bib.title: The Last AI Built by Humans: Toward Genuine Recursive Self-Improvement

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "The Last AI Built by Humans: Toward Genuine Recursive Self-Improvement", Yi Duan, Ying Liu, Zirui Tang, Haodong Chen, Jun Zhou et al. (Shanghai Jiao Tong Univ., Theseus Labs and others; corresponding author Xuanhe Zhou). arXiv:2609.11873v3 [cs.LG], 22 Sep 2026. Preprint survey.

COVERAGE: 337,695 chars extracted (79 pages). Read in full: chars 0-225,000 (abstract, body pp.1-49, start of references) and 271,500-337,695 (Appendices A, B, C). NOT read: chars ~228,000-271,500 (reference list, pp.~51-62; skimmed only the first ~20 entries, to find origins). Page 1 Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 are diagrams, so only their text labels were extracted. Section 4 says "Appendix??", a broken cross-reference.

IMPORTANT FRAMING FOR THE TARGET NOTE: the survey's levels are a ladder of how much of the *improvement* process the AI owns (RSI), not how much of the *operator's* job is handed off. It is a different axis from note 07's four rungs. It fits note 08 (self-improving loops) better, and gives note 07 a third, contrasting axis.

TAXONOMY (B0 plus L1-L5; each level adds one decision the AI takes over)
- B0, in-task: "output change without persistent system change". Non-RSI reference. Examples: Self-Refine, Reflexion, Tree of Thoughts. Experience is discarded after the task.
- L1, improvement execution: humans fix the objective, procedure and acceptance criteria; AI executes and the result persists. Example: FineWeb-Edu, Meta Capacity Efficiency repair skills. Boundary B0 to L1 is persistence.
- L2, improvement strategy: AI diagnoses and picks which intervention to try. Objective, task boundary and evaluation stay fixed. Examples: GEPA, ADAS, AFlow, AgentSquare, autoresearch, Self-Harness. Loop: "observe performance -> diagnose -> select how change -> instantiate and test -> retain or revert -> repeat".
- L3, learning-signal/experience acquisition: AI chooses what to learn from next. Examples: AZR, R-Zero, STP, VOYAGER, SIMA 2, SEAgent. Defining property: "learner-conditioned future experience acquisition".
- L4, environment/deployment adaptation: deployment feedback changes persistent state (memory, skills, harness, code, weights). Examples: Metis, HarnessDev, HDSO, PANDO, Tax AI. Humans keep objective, access boundaries, protected evaluation and release authority.
- L5, recursive inheritance: AI revises the mechanism that governs later improvement (improver, evaluator, research policy). Examples: STOP, Gödel Agent, DGM, HyperAgents, RQGM, A-Evolve-Training, AIDE2. Split into "structural L5" (change persists and controls a later round) and "effective L5" (it yields better successors under comparable budgets and independent assessment).
- Cross-level boundaries (p.35): B0-L1 persistence; L1-L2 strategy selection; L2-L3 learning agenda; L3-L4 persistent deployment adaptation; L4-L5 recursive inheritance.
- Improvement-loop vocabulary (2.2.1): AI system, system state, experience, target, improver, strategy, verifier, improvement, successor. Three questions per level: where does the loop close, what persists, which decisions stay external.
- Application regimes: science, embodied, software engineering, healthcare. Software engineering is "Mature L2, emerging L3, bounded structural L5" (Fig. 9).

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Higher autonomy does not mean a better improvement process.
   number: none
   quote: "a higher autonomy level does not by itself imply a better improvement process. Greater delegated authority can coexist with inefficient search, unreliable feedback, regression, evaluator exploitation, or poor transfer."
   where: Sec 3.7, p.35 (~char 141,000)
2. The evidence thins out toward the top levels: survey of 491 papers by level.
   number: L1 215 (43.8%), L2 155 (31.6%), L3 64 (13.0%), L4 28 (5.7%), L5 29 (5.9%)
   setup: the survey's own paper counting; percentages are by paper count.
   quote: "Papers 215 155 64 28 29 Percentage 43.8% 31.6% 13.0% 5.7% 5.9%" and "n = 491"
   where: Appendix A, Fig. 18, ~char 272,000
3. Humans keep the objective, protected evaluation and release authority at every level, including L5.
   quote: "Human designers still establish the overall mission, protected evaluation, editable components, and resource permissions, and may retain veto and deployment authority."
   where: Sec 3.6, p.31
4. Repeated evaluator access invites exploitation. Anthropic's automated research experiments reported seed cherry-picking and test-label extraction.
   number: none
   quote: "reported behaviors include random-seed cherry-picking, shortcut discovery, and attempted test-label extraction through repeated evaluator queries [20]. Once a benchmark is queried adaptively, it effectively becomes part of the optimization surface"
   where: Sec 3.3.4, p.21
5. Gödel Agent: persistence makes errors inheritable.
   number: 14 of 100 MGSM trials
   setup: Gödel Agent rewrites its own task policy and update logic.
   quote: "14 of 100 MGSM optimization trials ended below the initial policy's performance"
   where: Sec 3.6.1, p.33 (also 1.3)
6. Darwin Gödel Machine gain.
   number: 20% to 50%
   setup: SWE-bench subset; archive management and parent selection stay outside self-modification.
   quote: "raising performance on its SWE-bench subset from 20% to 50%, but its archive maintenance and parent-selection rules remain outside self-modification"
   where: Sec 1.3, p.4
7. L5 effectiveness is not established.
   (a) AIDE2: "Weco reports seven accepted improvements over 100 unattended steps and transfer to external tasks. Its stronger test of whether the evolved agent improves the outer search faster found no statistically significant efficiency advantage." (company-reported, p.34)
   (b) HyperAgents: "The longer, 200-iteration experiment did not establish a statistically significant final advantage for transferred initialization." (p.33)
   (c) Conclusion: "Statistically reliable accumulation across generations under comparable resources remains open [93, 94]." (p.35)
8. Red Queen Gödel Machine freezes the evaluator within an epoch and checks replacements against an independent anchor.
   number: 71.7% vs 69.9%
   setup: held-out Polyglot coding tasks, vs HGM-H; preprint, lower search-token use.
   quote: "the preprint reports a 71.7% pass rate against 69.9% for HGM-H, with lower search-token use"
   where: Sec 3.6.2, p.33
9. A-Evolve-Training.
   number: 0.80 to 0.86 vs 0.87 for the top human
   setup: four autonomous rounds on a 30B Nemotron model. The meta-agent revised the research policy when dev scores rose without external gains. The objective stayed human-defined.
   quote: "Across four autonomous rounds on a 30B Nemotron model, the external score rose from 0.80 to 0.86, compared with 0.87 for the top human submission [17]."
   where: Sec 1.2, p.4
10. Updating a harness is not the same as benefiting from it.
    number: none
    setup: fixed solve-evolve protocol, several backbones, three agent benchmarks.
    quote: "Updating ability is largely independent of base model capability, with a small model's updates yielding gains comparable to a frontier model's." Failures concentrate where "relevant artifacts are not activated, or they are activated but not faithfully followed."
    where: Sec 3.5.2, p.30
11. Skill libraries decay and need lifecycle governance.
    quote: "unbounded accumulation gradually degrades retrieval quality and stalls progress, often before the effect becomes visible in task scores" and "retiring skills too aggressively performs worse than leaving the library unguided."
    where: Sec 3.5.3, p.30 (Library Drift [152])
12. Gated promotion patterns: HDSO runs control vs treatment on the same tasks, scaled up in stages, then confirms on independent tasks. Tax AI keeps a human at the end: "Each fix arrives as a pull request for engineering review before release". ASPIRE uses a "score-gated controller rolls back any change whose verified score does not improve". Frontis uses three gates: regression safety, target achievement, robustness. (pp.30, 45)
13. Industry numbers, all company-reported, which the survey says are not equivalent to independent replication:
    - Humanlaya: key-defect rate 9.0% to 3.7%, human handling time 48 to 27 min/task. Setup: V0 vs V4 after four updates, same base model, 600 held-out task packages. quote: "decreased from 9.0% to 3.7%, while average human handling time fell from 48 to 27 minutes per task." (p.42)
    - Frontis: "216 improvement tasks involving 117 specialist agents, of which 63 completed at least one full evolution cycle"; scores 5.25 to 5.87 across 76 comparable tasks; "approximately 20% faster evolution" after 100+ tasks of meta-experience. (p.46)
    - Xiaohongshu: score_mean@16 2.211 to 2.366 (+7.0%). In-video feed ~+13.1% on a small offline eval (470 vs 447 samples). Survey says gains in click-through or conversion are not established. (p.41)
    - Lark: automated evaluator "approximately 84% agreement with human judgments". (p.40)
    - ModelBest ForgeTrain: matched Megatron-LM v0.15 "within roughly 8 hours", reportedly surpassed it in 1.5-2.5 days. (p.43)
14. Capability headroom is uneven (393 model-benchmark observations, HCI metric, models 2023 to Sept 2026). 2026 HCI values: grad science 85.8, software engineering 52.6, search/terminal 56.8, tool agents 39.9. quote: "Software engineering reaches an HCI of 52.6 in 2026, search and terminal agents reach 56.8, and tool agents reach 39.9." The post-2026 "RSI extension" curve (Eq. 4, 22% of remaining gap closed) is explicitly illustrative, not measured. (p.9)
15. Burden figures: agentic workloads use "approximately four times as many tokens as ordinary chat, rising to about fifteen times for multi-agent systems" (citing Anthropic). (p.3)

LIMITS
- The authors concede the L5 evidence is "concentrated in bounded prototypes", L3-L4 are "domain-dependent", and L4 evaluations "cover bounded task streams and limited combinations of models, tasks, and environments".
- The L5 test proposals (goal selection, stopping) are "proposed requirements ... rather than capabilities established by existing RSI benchmarks."
- Figure 6 positions are "an interpretive synthesis ... not quantitative measurements". Level labels in Table 13 are the authors' mapping, not the companies'.
- The survey's coverage is company blogs, preprints and technical reports, so provenance varies. Some chapter-5 authors are affiliated with the surveyed companies (Theseus, Lark, Humanlaya, ModelBest, Frontis, ByteDance, Xiaohongshu, Tencent).
- It does not give a single comparable benchmark across levels.
- Many cited items are 2026 preprints I could not check against the reference list.

BUILDS ON (as printed): Schmidhuber 2003 Gödel machines; Zelikman et al. 2024 STOP; Zhang et al. DGM (ICLR 2026); Yin et al. 2025 Gödel Agent; Hu et al. ADAS; Zhang et al. AFlow; Tao et al. 2024 "A survey on self-evolution of LLMs" (arXiv 2404.14387, the same survey note 07 already cites); Gao et al. 2026 self-evolving agents survey; Fang et al. 2025; Ren et al. 2026; Wang et al. Voyager; Wang et al. POET. The survey says these taxonomies "organize work by stages of self-evolution, update objects, timing, or technical mechanisms", whereas it uses who decides.

CODE: none in the paper. Useful verbatim loop strings:
- L1: "receive improvement objective -> execute prescribed procedure -> produce improvement -> update system state -> process the next task -> repeat"
- L4: "observe deployment interaction -> propose persistent adaptation -> revise agent components -> validate and retain -> reuse in later tasks -> collect new feedback and repeat"
- Software engineering: "Development Challenge -> Agent-Level Modification -> Repository-Grounded Trial -> Regression-Aware Selection -> Versioned Inheritance"

FIGURES (candidates)
- Fig. 2 (p.5), "Loop Patterns of Five Levels": the strongest figure. Grey frames are human-controlled, green are inside the RSI loop, orange marks the component taken over at each level. It shows autonomy as a growing green region. It is the closest analogue to note 07's ladder.
- Fig. 1 (p.2): overview of levels with representative systems (dense).
- Fig. 8 (p.32): L4 fixed process vs L5 process revised and inherited.
- Fig. 7 (p.27): L4 pagination example with distill, revise, select-and-retain; HDSO control vs treatment.
- Fig. 4 (p.19): L2 strategy selection. Fig. 5 (p.23): L3 with the code-reasoning and Minecraft cactus examples.
- Fig. 9 (p.36): per-domain level reached; Fig. 18 (p.63): paper counts by level.
- Table 8 (p.35): L5 evaluation dimensions: adaptivity, retention, transfer, efficiency, stability, meta-recursion.
- Table 1 (p.12): RSI vs continual learning, AutoML, agentic AI.

PROBLEMS: Text extraction is clean, apart from ligatures and symbols in Table 13 (a "/gl⌢be" glyph for link icons) and some jumbled figure labels. No embedded instructions found. Reference list pp.51-62 largely unread. The quotes come from the pypdf extraction, which is saved at /tmp/duan.txt (disposable). The survey does not discuss operator-facing autonomy rungs (/goal, /loop, /schedule) at all, so mapping to note 07 is the caller's inference. The closest overlap is its human-retained authority and its verifier-gating of retention, which echoes "earn each handoff with a verifier". Dates are 2026 and preprint status is unverified.
